# SERVICE THAT FITS THE MARKET
## A regional operating framework for customer service, satisfaction and loyalty
**Proposal for regional leadership and the Global Service Council | v1.0**

**Decision sought:** adoption of (a) the four-layer service structure and decision rights, (b) the contact-intent taxonomy as the design unit, (c) the twelve intervention tracks, and (d) funding for the Diagnostic Gate. **All quantities are design targets calibrated at the Diagnostic Gate and returned for approval before anything is promised to customers.**

---

## The answer in one paragraph

**Stop trying to improve "customer service" and start eliminating the reasons customers have to contact us.** Regional satisfaction problems are almost never solved by adding headcount, extending hours or bolting on a chatbot; they are solved by separating three fundamentally different things that our current operation blends into one queue: **failure demand** (contacts caused by our own defects — wrong ETAs, opaque returns, failed payments), **value demand** (contacts where the customer legitimately needs help or advice), and **relationship moments** (contacts where the customer's trust is either won or destroyed). Each requires a different design. Therefore: adopt a **four-layer model** — a thin, non-waivable **Service Spine** (seven promises that make us one brand); a **Regional Dial** set by [Market M] against a published dossier of language, channel, payment, logistics and regulatory realities; a **Journey Charter** per contact-intent family, owned by a named cross-functional owner with authority over the upstream defect, not just the queue; and a **Frontline Authority** layer that gives the person actually talking to the customer a published, funded right to resolve. Work the twelve tracks in §5 in sequence — **failure demand first, because it is the cheapest satisfaction gain we will ever buy** — and measure with a metric triad (§8) that makes it impossible to hide a bad experience behind a good average. **One constraint governs everything: the Resolution Rule (§3) — every contact is resolved at the earliest point that can see the customer's whole problem, and no later.**

---

## §0 Scope and status

### 0.1 Status of the numbers

Every percentage, hour, currency value, SLA and threshold below is a **design target for calibration, not a measured value**, and is marked *[target]* on first use. They exist because a proposal with no numbers cannot be argued with. **The Diagnostic Gate (§9) replaces them with measured values**; leadership approves the calibrated set before any customer-facing commitment is made.

Market-specific variables — language(s) and dialects, dominant messaging platform, payment mix, address conventions, delivery-partner mix, consumer-protection law, cultural norms around complaint and confrontation — are deliberately left as **[Market M variables]** and filled at the Diagnostic Gate. A framework that pretends to know these in advance is the first cause of the problem we are trying to fix.

### 0.2 Who this covers

"Customer service" is routinely used as a synonym for "the contact centre." That framing guarantees failure, because most of what determines satisfaction happens before anyone contacts us and is owned by teams who never see a ticket.

| Population | Illustrative share of contact volume *[target]* | What "better service" means here | Governed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Self-resolvers** | ~[55]% | Never needing us; and when they do, resolving it themselves *in seconds, inside the app* | §5 Tracks 1–4 |
| **B. Assisted resolvers** | ~[35]% | Reaching a competent human fast, once, in their language, with authority to fix it | §5 Tracks 5–8 |
| **C. High-stakes / high-emotion** | ~[10]% | Being *held* — ownership, proactive updates, real remedy, follow-up | §5 Tracks 9–12 |
| **D. Silent dissatisfied** | Invisible in ticket data; possibly [2–4]× population C | Being *detected* without contacting us at all | §8.3 |

**Rule of the document:** population D is the one that churns. Any metric set that cannot see it is a vanity metric. Every reporting cut in §8 includes a silent-signal panel.

Also in scope, and usually omitted: **the frontline agents themselves** (§6). Agent experience is not a welfare topic; it is the single largest controllable input to customer satisfaction, and in this market it is currently a bottleneck.

---

## §1 Stating the problem correctly

The regional feedback says "support is not meeting expectations." That sentence contains no diagnosis. Reframe it:

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| How do we improve our support channels? | Why are customers contacting us at all, and which contacts are our own defects? |
| How do we reduce response time? | How do we reduce *time to resolution* — and how often do we make the customer come back a second time? |
| Should we add a chatbot? | Which contacts have low consequence and high machine confidence — and which must never touch automation? |
| Are customers satisfied? | Are they *returning*, buying across categories, and telling us the truth — and which segments have gone quiet? |
| What's our CSAT? | What is our CSAT **for the journeys we handle worst**, in the local language, at the local peak? |
| Why is this market underperforming? | Which of our global defaults are simply wrong here — channel, language, payment, returns, tone, hours? |

**Corollary 1 — Contact volume is a defect signal, not a workload forecast.** The default operational reflex is to staff to demand. The correct first reflex is to ask which demand should not exist. Every recurring contact reason is an unpaid invoice from another department.

**Corollary 2 — Most regional dissatisfaction is not a service problem.** It is a **promise problem** (ETAs we cannot keep), a **legibility problem** (policies written for a different market), a **language problem** (translated, not localised), a **channel problem** (we offer email; they live on messaging), or an **authority problem** (agents who must escalate to help). Fixing these is cheaper than expanding the centre, and it compounds. **Sequence them first.**

**Corollary 3 — Satisfaction and loyalty are not the same objective.** Satisfaction is the absence of friction. Loyalty is the presence of reciprocity — a memory of being treated well when it would have been easy to treat us badly. A programme that only removes friction produces indifferent customers who leave for a discount. Tracks 9–12 exist for this reason.

---

## §2 What we are optimising for

**A gate, not a priority — Regulatory, data and consumer-protection integrity.** No arrangement that breaches [Market M] consumer law (return windows, refund timelines, warranty duties, cooling-off rights), data-residency or privacy rules, marketing-consent rules, accessibility obligations, or any outsourcing/labour agreement covering frontline staff. Applied as pass/fail *before* options are compared. Legal and DPO hold a veto, not an opinion. Automated decisioning that affects a customer's money is in scope of this gate.

**The five ranked objectives**, in priority order when they conflict:

| Rank | Objective | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Trust** | Customers believe our promises (ETA accuracy, refund actually arriving on the day stated) and believe we will make things right |
| **2** | **Effective resolution** | The customer's problem is *gone*, first time, without a second contact |
| **3** | **Effortlessness** | Time and steps the customer spends, measured in *their* terms, not ours |
| **4** | **Relationship depth** | Repeat purchase, category expansion, willingness to be contacted, advocacy |
| **5** | **Cost to serve** | Fully-loaded cost per resolved contact, and per *retained* customer |

Trust outranks resolution because a fast fix inside a system that lies about delivery dates buys nothing. Cost is last because savings taken out of trust are borrowed, not earned — and in this market, evidently, already overdrawn.

### 2.1 Adjudication

- Conflicts are decided by the **Regional Service Council** (§7.1) on a written submission naming the objectives in tension, the evidence, and the customer population affected.
- **Burden of proof sits with the lower-ranked objective.** A containment or automation proposal that reduces trust must quantify both the saving and the harm and propose mitigation. "It deflects [X]% of contacts" is not an argument; it is a number awaiting an argument.
- Any decision that overrides objective 1 requires **Regional MD + Global Service Head** sign-off and entry in the Exception Register with a review date.
- The Council publishes its decisions. Precedent is how a federated service model stays coherent without a 400-page script library.

---

## §3 The Resolution Rule and the four layers

> **Resolution Rule:** Every customer problem is resolved at the earliest point that can see the whole problem — and no later. Every *policy* about resolution is set at the lowest layer that can see every customer it affects — and no lower.

| Layer | Owner | Scope | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Service Spine** | Global Service Council | 7 promises. Universal, non-waivable. | Annual |
| **Regional Dial** | [Market M] leadership + CX + Legal + Logistics | Channel mix, languages and dialects, hours, remedy menu and values, returns/refund mechanics, payment-failure handling, tone-of-voice guide, escalation ladder, partner SLAs | Quarterly |
| **Journey Charter** | Named cross-functional Journey Owner per contact-intent family (§4) | Root-cause backlog, self-service flow, automation boundary, agent playbook, target metrics, defect SLA on upstream teams | Monthly review, published |
| **Frontline Authority** | Agent, within published guardrails | Resolve, refund, replace, waive, expedite, gift — up to a funded discretion limit, without escalation | Continuous; audited monthly |

### 3.1 The Service Spine (adopt or amend; do not expand)

**P1 — We tell the truth about time.** Every promise we display (delivery, refund, response, repair) is a commitment we measure ourselves against publicly, with an honest confidence range rather than an optimistic point estimate. Under-promise; over-deliver.

**P2 — One contact, one owner.** A customer never re-explains their problem. Ownership transfers with full context; the customer is never the integration layer between our departments.

**P3 — Never a dead end.** Every automated interaction has a visible, one-tap route to a human. Automation may triage, draft, translate and act; it may not trap.

**P4 — The frontline can fix things.** Every agent has published authority to resolve up to a defined value without permission. Escalation is a design failure, tracked as such.

**P5 — Local by default, not translated.** Language, tone, channel, examples, payment methods, address handling and holiday calendars are set locally. Global templates are a starting point, never a requirement.

**P6 — Accessible to everyone who buys from us.** Low-bandwidth paths, voice options where literacy or connectivity demand it, screen-reader compliance, and a channel that works on the devices our customers actually own.

**P7 — Every recurring contact reason has an owner outside the contact centre.** Service reports the defect; the defect's owner is accountable for eliminating it, on a clock.

Seven is the ceiling. Anything added must be simultaneously true, legal, affordable and culturally legible in every market we operate.

---

## §4 The design unit: contact intents, not channels

Organising service by channel (phone team, email team, chat team) guarantees inconsistency, because the *same* problem gets a different answer depending on where the customer knocked. Organise instead by **intent**, and route intent to the treatment it deserves.

| # | Intent | Discriminating test | Correct treatment | Automation suitability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **I1** | **Status anxiety** — "where is my order?" | Customer wants information we already hold | **Eliminate**: proactive push, accurate tracking, live ETA | Full — but the real answer is prevention |
| **I2** | **Transaction change** — reschedule, reroute, cancel, address fix | Customer wants a *state change*, not advice | **Self-serve action**, one tap, instant confirmation | Full, if the flow *acts* rather than explains |
| **I3** | **Something is broken** — wrong, damaged, missing, late, payment failed | A promise was broken | **Human or high-confidence auto-remedy, plus root-cause capture** | Partial; consequence is high |
| **I4** | **Advice and decision help** — sizing, fit, compatibility, comparison | Customer needs judgement to buy | **Assisted commerce** — expert humans, community, rich content | Assist only; converts revenue |
| **I5** | **Trust rupture** — anger, unfairness, repeated failure, public complaint, vulnerability | The relationship is at stake | **Named senior owner, generous fast remedy, follow-up** | **Never automate** |

**The two intents teams confuse:** I1 and I3. "Where is my order" *after* a missed promise is not I1 — it is I3 wearing I1's clothes, and answering it with a tracking link is how a recoverable failure becomes churn. Detection logic for this is a Diagnostic Gate deliverable.

**Design implication:** I1 and I2 are, we believe, the majority of current contact volume in [Market M] — *this is a hypothesis, not a finding*, and it is the Diagnostic Gate's first test. If confirmed, the highest-return investment is not the contact centre at all.

---

## §5 The twelve intervention tracks

Ordered by sequence, not by ambition. Tracks 1–4 pay for the rest.

### Wave 1 — Eliminate failure demand *(weeks 0–12)*

**Track 1 — Contact-reason forensics and defect ownership.**
Re-code the last [12] months of contacts into the I1–I5 taxonomy plus a root-cause layer (carrier, catalogue, payment, policy, UX, our own message). Publish a weekly **Top 20 Contact Reasons** board with a named owner *outside* service for each, a defect SLA *[target: root cause fixed or mitigation shipped within 60 days]*, and a visible cost-of-failure figure per reason. **Innovation is not required here; accountability is.** Expected volume reduction: *[target: 20–30% within two quarters]*.

**Track 2 — Honest promises engine.**
Replace optimistic single-date ETAs with locally calibrated, confidence-ranged promises computed per postcode/partner/product/season. Deliberately pad the customer-facing promise while optimising the internal target; measure **promise-kept rate**, not average delivery time. In markets with volatile last-mile, this single change typically moves satisfaction more than any contact-centre investment.

**Track 3 — Proactive disruption service.**
Detect the failure before the customer does — carrier exception, customs hold, weather event, stock-out, failed payment, address ambiguity — and reach out first with (a) what happened, (b) what we've already done, (c) two choices, (d) a remedy already applied where we were at fault. **The default is not "notify"; it is "notify and resolve in the same message."** Preventing an I1/I3 contact is worth several times containing one.

**Track 4 — Self-service that acts.**
Retire FAQ-as-service. Every I2 intent becomes a one-tap action in-app and in the order confirmation: reschedule, reroute, change address, cancel, return, exchange, split delivery, refund-to-original-method. Embedded contextually at the point of friction, not buried in a help centre. Target: *[80]% of I2 resolved without human contact and without customer effort exceeding [3] taps.*

### Wave 2 — Rebuild assisted service for this market *(weeks 8–24)*

**Track 5 — Channel realism.**
Meet customers where they already are. Move the primary assisted channel to **[Market M's dominant messaging platform]** with full commerce and identity integration, asynchronous by design, threaded so history persists and P2 is structurally guaranteed. Retain voice for I3/I5 and for segments that prefer it; retain a low-bandwidth path. **Do not add channels — replace them.** Channel proliferation is how consistency dies.

**Track 6 — Localisation, not translation.**
Native speakers of [Market M languages and principal dialects], locally written tone-of-voice guide (directness, formality, apology conventions, how complaint is culturally expressed), local holiday and peak calendars, local payment-failure playbooks (including cash-on-delivery, instalments, wallet mechanics as applicable), local address-normalisation logic, local returns network (partner stores, lockers, pickup points) instead of an imported courier-only model. Hire a small number of **service designers who are from this market**, not global staff on rotation.

**Track 7 — The AI/human boundary, drawn on two axes.**
Automate on **confidence × consequence**, never on cost alone.

| | Low consequence | High consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **High machine confidence** | **Automate fully** (I1, I2) | **Automate the action, notify a human owner** (auto-refund with audit) |
| **Low machine confidence** | **Automate triage; human resolves** | **Human only, senior, no bot in the path** (I5) |

# WHERE AND HOW WE WORK
## A global operating framework for flexible work
**Executive Committee decision document | v2.0**
**Decision sought: adoption of the *structure* and the decision rights. All quantities are calibrated at Gate 1 and returned to this Committee for approval.**

---

## The answer in one paragraph

**Stop trying to write one work policy for the whole company.** A single global rule — "three days in office," "remote-first," "hybrid" — will be simultaneously too loose for the teams that need co-presence to function and too tight for the teams that don't, and it will be illegal, unaffordable or culturally illegible in a meaningful share of our countries. Instead, adopt a **federated model with three layers**: a thin, non-waivable **Global Spine** (eight commitments that make us one company); a **Country Dial** set by each market against a published dossier of legal, infrastructural and normative constraints; and a **Team Charter** — the real unit of decision — written by every team of roughly 6–15 people and reviewed twice a year. Work is designed against **five work modes and two overlays** (§4), not against days of the week. Offices are re-typed from desk inventory into a **four-format portfolio** whose feasibility depends on one piece of machinery we have never had: **cross-team anchor-day allocation** (§9.2). Roughly [X]% of our workforce cannot choose where they work at all; they are in scope from page one, not as an afterthought (§6). Fairness — proximity bias, geographic pay, apprenticeship — is engineered explicitly (§11), and output measurement is fixed *before* flexibility scales, because otherwise presence quietly becomes the proxy again (§12). **One constraint governs everything: the Subsidiarity Rule (§3) — each decision is made at the lowest layer that can see every person it affects, and no lower.**

---

## §0 Scope and status

### 0.1 Status of the numbers

Every ratio, day-count, square-metre figure, stipend value and threshold in this document is a **design target for calibration, not a measured value**, and is marked *[target]* on first use in each section. They are included because a framework with no numbers cannot be argued with, and an unarguable framework cannot be improved. **Gate 1 (§16) replaces them with measured values**; the Committee approves the calibrated set before any policy is communicated to employees.

What we are asking the Committee to adopt today is: the three-layer structure, the eight Spine commitments, the five modes, the four office formats, the decision-rights matrix (Appendix C), the gate sequence, and the funding of Gate 1.

### 0.2 Who this covers

The phrase "future of work" has been used inside the company as a synonym for "hybrid office work." That framing excludes a large minority — possibly a majority — of our people, and it is the fastest route to a two-class company.

| Population | Illustrative share *[target — Gate 1 to measure]* | What flexibility means here | Governed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Location-flexible** | ~[40]% | Where and when, within team and country limits | §§3–5, 7–12 |
| **B. Fixed-location** — manufacturing, warehouse, retail, lab, clinical, site security, catering, field maintenance | ~[45]% | **When**, not where: schedule predictability, shift choice, roster self-scheduling, compressed weeks, time-in-lieu, leave access | §6 (parallel framework, equal status) |
| **C. Mixed** — field service, sales, engineers with lab or site dependencies, plant supervisors | ~[15]% | Site-anchored days plus flexible remainder; the *anchor* is set by the site, the remainder by the Charter | §6.3 |

**Rule of the document:** wherever this framework grants something to population A, §6 states the equivalent grant to B and C, or explains why no equivalent exists. Wherever we report a fairness metric (§11.4), all three populations appear in the cut. A benefit that only knowledge workers can consume is not a benefit; it is a differential.

---

## §1 Stating the problem correctly

The debate has been framed as *remote vs. office*. That axis is unhelpful, because it treats location as the variable when location is a **consequence**.

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| How many days in the office? | What work do we do that is *degraded* by distance, and how much of it is there? |
| Is remote work productive? | Which roles have output that is legible without co-presence — and which have we simply never learned to measure? (§12) |
| How do we get people back? | What must the office be *good at* that a home desk isn't, and are our buildings currently good at it? |
| What's our policy? | Who decides, at what layer, with what evidence, and who hears the appeal? (§3, §15) |

**Corollary 1.** Attendance is not a goal. It is an input we may or may not need. A policy expressed *purely* as a day-count is a confession that the analysis wasn't done. (Day-count *bands* have exactly one legitimate use — real-estate planning and legal negotiation. That use is fenced in §7.3.)

**Corollary 2.** Most of the pain reported as "hybrid isn't working" is not about location. It is about **meeting load, unclear decision rights, documentation debt, time-zone tax and untrained managers**. Those are fixable independent of where anyone sits; they are cheaper than real estate; and they compound. **Sequence them first** (§16, Gate 2 wave 1).

---

## §2 What we are optimising for

Named explicitly, because unnamed objectives get traded away silently.

**A gate, not a priority:** *Legal, tax and collective-agreement integrity.* No arrangement that creates permanent-establishment exposure, misclassifies employment, breaches a works-council agreement or violates working-time law. This is not ranked against anything; it is a pass/fail test applied before options are compared. Legal and Tax hold a veto, not an opinion.

**The five ranked objectives**, in priority order when they conflict:

| Rank | Objective | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Equity of opportunity** | A person's promotion odds are not predicted by their distance from a headquarters, their work pattern, or their population (A/B/C) |
| **2** | **Output quality and speed** | Team-level delivery against commitments, measured per §12 |
| **3** | **Cohesion** | Enough shared context that the company can change direction without fracturing |
| **4** | **Talent access** | Hiring and retention in labour markets a full-return policy would close to us |
| **5** | **Cost discipline** | Real estate and workplace spend per employee, against the §14 bridge |

Equity outranks output because equity failures are slow, compounding and legally actionable, while output problems are visible and correctable. Cost is last because savings taken out of cohesion and equity are borrowed, not earned.

### 2.1 Adjudication — who breaks the tie

An unarbitrated priority list is decorative. Therefore:

- Conflicts between objectives are decided by the **Work Design Council** (§15.1) on a written submission that names the objectives in tension, the evidence, and the population affected.
- **Burden of proof sits with the lower-ranked objective.** A cost proposal that reduces equity or cohesion must quantify the saving *and* the harm, and propose mitigation. "It's cheaper" is not an argument; it is a number awaiting an argument.
- Any decision that overrides objective 1 requires **CPO + CEO** sign-off and is entered in the Exception Register (§15.3) with a review date.
- The Council publishes its decisions internally. Precedent is how a federated model stays coherent without a rulebook.

---

## §3 The Subsidiarity Rule and the three layers

> **Subsidiarity Rule:** Every decision about where and how work happens is made at the lowest layer that can see every person it affects — and no lower.

A decision affecting one team's week belongs to that team. A decision affecting statutory rights belongs to the country. A decision affecting whether two teams on different continents can ship together belongs to the centre. Pushing a decision *up* costs speed and fit; pushing it *down* costs coherence and manufactures local unfairness.

| Layer | Owner | Scope | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Global Spine** | Executive Committee | 8 commitments. Universal, non-waivable. | Annual review |
| **Country Dial** | Country lead + HR + Legal, with works council where applicable | Legal floor, stipend values, office footprint and format mix, planning band, local core hours, right-to-disconnect implementation, language of record | Semi-annual |
| **Team Charter** | Team lead with the team | Mode profile, together-time and its purpose, core overlap, response-time norms, meeting inventory, decision protocol, onboarding, inclusion check | Semi-annual, published |

Full decision rights, including who may *not* decide what, are in **Appendix C**.

### 3.1 The Global Spine (adopt or amend; do not expand)

**S1 — Purpose before place.** Every requirement to be somewhere must name the work mode (§4) it serves. "Because it's Tuesday" is not a reason.

**S2 — Every team has a written, published Charter.** Unwritten norms are how proximity bias enters a company. If it isn't written, it isn't a norm; it's a hazard.

**S3 — Written-first for decisions, specs and context.** These live in a durable, searchable, permissioned place. *Scope limit:* S3 governs **decisions, specifications and context only**. It explicitly does **not** apply to 1:1s, coaching, sensitive feedback, performance conversations, wellbeing discussions or relationship time — documenting those would be both chilling and, in several jurisdictions, unlawful. The old formulation ("a meeting with no artefact did not happen") is withdrawn as absolutist; the replacement test is: *if a decision was made and is not written down, it will be re-made.*

**S4 — Meetings are opt-in for information, opt-out for decisions.** No standing meeting survives two quarters without explicit renewal by its owner in the Charter's meeting inventory.

**S5 — One time-zone tax, shared.** Recurring cross-region meetings rotate their inconvenience; no region is permanently the one dialling in at 22:00.
*Exception path (mandatory, because rotation is sometimes impossible):* where the counterparty is a customer, a market open, a regulator or a plant shift, a **Standing Unsociable-Hours Exception** may be granted by the regional leader for ≤12 months, renewable, entered in the Exception Register, and only with one of four compensating remedies named: (a) follow-the-sun redesign so the handoff replaces the meeting; (b) hiring or relocating for overlap; (c) time-in-lieu at a published rate; (d) an unsociable-hours allowance where local law and practice support it. An exception with no remedy is refused.

**S6 — Same job, same access.** Location and work pattern do not change eligibility for projects, promotion, sponsorship, budget or information. Where location changes *compensation*, the rule is published, zone-based and applied mechanically (§11.2).

**S7 — A baseline environment guarantee, for everyone.** Every employee has a safe, connected, ergonomically adequate place to work — at home, in a company office, at a paid third space, or **at their site**, at company cost, at levels set by the Country Dial. For population B this reads as facilities standards: rest space, lockers, connectivity, decent break areas, and equivalent per-head workplace spend. Population B must not fund population A's stipends out of its own neglected estate.

**S8 — Nothing that breaks local law, tax status or a collective agreement.** No exceptions, no goodwill workarounds, no "just for this one hire."

Eight is the ceiling. Every additional global rule must be true simultaneously in Lagos, Stuttgart, Bengaluru, São Paulo, Osaka and Salt Lake City — and very few things are.

---

## §4 The five work modes and two overlays

Modes, not days, are the design unit. Sort a team's actual month into these five, apply the overlays, and its Charter largely writes itself.

### 4.1 The five modes (mutually exclusive; every hour lands in exactly one)

| # | Mode | Discriminating test | Distance sensitivity | Best setting | Primary enabler |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **M1** | **Deep focus** | One person producing; interruption is the enemy | **Negative** — co-presence usually *harms* it | **Any environment the individual controls and can reach reliably** — home study, quiet office zone, or a Touchdown site (§9.1) where home is not viable | Calendar protection; do-not-disturb norms |
| **M2** | **Convergent work** | *Someone has to change their mind or merge two positions.* Known problem, needs a decision | Low–moderate | Anywhere with good tooling; short sync after async pre-read | Pre-read + 30-min call + written decision |
| **M3** | **Divergent work** | *Nobody knows the answer yet.* Ambiguity, generation, productive conflict, whiteboarding | **High** | Same room, writable walls, 2–6 hour blocks | In-person workshop; digital canvas as an honest second-best |
| **M4** | **Apprenticeship and tacit transfer** | *Someone is learning judgement that isn't written down.* | **Very high** | Same room, sustained, with unscheduled overhearing | Co-location blocks; work-alongs; senior time budget (§11.3) |
| **M5** | **Coordination and handoff** | *Someone needs to know something at the right time.* Status, dependencies, handoffs | Low, **if disciplined** | Nowhere in particular | Written status; overlap window; single source of truth |

M2 vs M5 is the distinction teams get wrong. **Changing a mind is M2. Transferring knowledge is M5.** If a recurring meeting only transmits information, it is M5 and should be a document.

### 4.2 The two overlays (not modes — do not allocate percentages to them)

- **Overlay T — Trust formation.** Relational credit is an *investment* that makes M2 and M3 cheap, not a mode of work. It is therefore handled as a **named budget and cadence** — offsites, shared meals, travel — owned at the Charter level and funded per §14.3. Design target *[target]*: every distributed team is physically together **at least twice a year**, and no employee goes **more than six months** without being in a room with colleagues. Treating trust as a byproduct is how distributed teams die quietly.
- **Overlay C — Customer, site and shift override.** For customer-facing, field and site-dependent work, location is determined by the customer or the asset, not by us. Overlay C **overrides** the mode's preferred setting for the hours it applies to; the underlying mode is still recorded (a salesperson doing discovery in a client's boardroom is doing M3 under Overlay C). This eliminates the double-counting that a "customer-facing mode" would have guaranteed.

### 4.3 Design implications

Suggest innovative approaches and improvements for customer service in a regional market to increase customer satisfaction and build stronger customer relationships.

# SERVICE THAT FITS THE MARKET
## A regional operating framework for customer service, satisfaction and loyalty
**Proposal for regional leadership and the Global Service Council | v1.0**

**Decision sought:** adoption of (a) the four-layer service structure and decision rights, (b) the contact-intent taxonomy as the design unit, (c) the twelve intervention tracks, and (d) funding for the Diagnostic Gate. **All quantities are design targets calibrated at the Diagnostic Gate and returned for approval before anything is promised to customers.**

---

## The answer in one paragraph

**Stop trying to improve "customer service" and start eliminating the reasons customers have to contact us.** Regional satisfaction problems are almost never solved by adding headcount, extending hours or bolting on a chatbot; they are solved by separating three fundamentally different things that our current operation blends into one queue: **failure demand** (contacts caused by our own defects — wrong ETAs, opaque returns, failed payments), **value demand** (contacts where the customer legitimately needs help or advice), and **relationship moments** (contacts where the customer's trust is either won or destroyed). Each requires a different design. Therefore: adopt a **four-layer model** — a thin, non-waivable **Service Spine** (seven promises that make us one brand); a **Regional Dial** set by [Market M] against a published dossier of language, channel, payment, logistics and regulatory realities; a **Journey Charter** per contact-intent family, owned by a named cross-functional owner with authority over the upstream defect, not just the queue; and a **Frontline Authority** layer that gives the person actually talking to the customer a published, funded right to resolve. Work the twelve tracks in §5 in sequence — **failure demand first, because it is the cheapest satisfaction gain we will ever buy** — and measure with a metric triad (§8) that makes it impossible to hide a bad experience behind a good average. **One constraint governs everything: the Resolution Rule (§3) — every contact is resolved at the earliest point that can see the customer's whole problem, and no later.**

---

## §0 Scope and status

### 0.1 Status of the numbers

Every percentage, hour, currency value, SLA and threshold below is a **design target for calibration, not a measured value**, and is marked *[target]* on first use. They exist because a proposal with no numbers cannot be argued with. **The Diagnostic Gate (§9) replaces them with measured values**; leadership approves the calibrated set before any customer-facing commitment is made.

Market-specific variables — language(s) and dialects, dominant messaging platform, payment mix, address conventions, delivery-partner mix, consumer-protection law, cultural norms around complaint and confrontation — are deliberately left as **[Market M variables]** and filled at the Diagnostic Gate. A framework that pretends to know these in advance is the first cause of the problem we are trying to fix.

### 0.2 Who this covers

"Customer service" is routinely used as a synonym for "the contact centre." That framing guarantees failure, because most of what determines satisfaction happens before anyone contacts us and is owned by teams who never see a ticket.

| Population | Illustrative share of contact volume *[target]* | What "better service" means here | Governed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Self-resolvers** | ~[55]% | Never needing us; and when they do, resolving it themselves *in seconds, inside the app* | §5 Tracks 1–4 |
| **B. Assisted resolvers** | ~[35]% | Reaching a competent human fast, once, in their language, with authority to fix it | §5 Tracks 5–8 |
| **C. High-stakes / high-emotion** | ~[10]% | Being *held* — ownership, proactive updates, real remedy, follow-up | §5 Tracks 9–12 |
| **D. Silent dissatisfied** | Invisible in ticket data; possibly [2–4]× population C | Being *detected* without contacting us at all | §8.3 |

**Rule of the document:** population D is the one that churns. Any metric set that cannot see it is a vanity metric. Every reporting cut in §8 includes a silent-signal panel.

Also in scope, and usually omitted: **the frontline agents themselves** (§6). Agent experience is not a welfare topic; it is the single largest controllable input to customer satisfaction, and in this market it is currently a bottleneck.

---

## §1 Stating the problem correctly

The regional feedback says "support is not meeting expectations." That sentence contains no diagnosis. Reframe it:

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| How do we improve our support channels? | Why are customers contacting us at all, and which contacts are our own defects? |
| How do we reduce response time? | How do we reduce *time to resolution* — and how often do we make the customer come back a second time? |
| Should we add a chatbot? | Which contacts have low consequence and high machine confidence — and which must never touch automation? |
| Are customers satisfied? | Are they *returning*, buying across categories, and telling us the truth — and which segments have gone quiet? |
| What's our CSAT? | What is our CSAT **for the journeys we handle worst**, in the local language, at the local peak? |
| Why is this market underperforming? | Which of our global defaults are simply wrong here — channel, language, payment, returns, tone, hours? |

**Corollary 1 — Contact volume is a defect signal, not a workload forecast.** The default operational reflex is to staff to demand. The correct first reflex is to ask which demand should not exist. Every recurring contact reason is an unpaid invoice from another department.

**Corollary 2 — Most regional dissatisfaction is not a service problem.** It is a **promise problem** (ETAs we cannot keep), a **legibility problem** (policies written for a different market), a **language problem** (translated, not localised), a **channel problem** (we offer email; they live on messaging), or an **authority problem** (agents who must escalate to help). Fixing these is cheaper than expanding the centre, and it compounds. **Sequence them first.**

**Corollary 3 — Satisfaction and loyalty are not the same objective.** Satisfaction is the absence of friction. Loyalty is the presence of reciprocity — a memory of being treated well when it would have been easy to treat us badly. A programme that only removes friction produces indifferent customers who leave for a discount. Tracks 9–12 exist for this reason.

---

## §2 What we are optimising for

**A gate, not a priority — Regulatory, data and consumer-protection integrity.** No arrangement that breaches [Market M] consumer law (return windows, refund timelines, warranty duties, cooling-off rights), data-residency or privacy rules, marketing-consent rules, accessibility obligations, or any outsourcing/labour agreement covering frontline staff. Applied as pass/fail *before* options are compared. Legal and DPO hold a veto, not an opinion. Automated decisioning that affects a customer's money is in scope of this gate.

**The five ranked objectives**, in priority order when they conflict:

| Rank | Objective | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Trust** | Customers believe our promises (ETA accuracy, refund actually arriving on the day stated) and believe we will make things right |
| **2** | **Effective resolution** | The customer's problem is *gone*, first time, without a second contact |
| **3** | **Effortlessness** | Time and steps the customer spends, measured in *their* terms, not ours |
| **4** | **Relationship depth** | Repeat purchase, category expansion, willingness to be contacted, advocacy |
| **5** | **Cost to serve** | Fully-loaded cost per resolved contact, and per *retained* customer |

Trust outranks resolution because a fast fix inside a system that lies about delivery dates buys nothing. Cost is last because savings taken out of trust are borrowed, not earned — and in this market, evidently, already overdrawn.

### 2.1 Adjudication

- Conflicts are decided by the **Regional Service Council** (§7.1) on a written submission naming the objectives in tension, the evidence, and the customer population affected.
- **Burden of proof sits with the lower-ranked objective.** A containment or automation proposal that reduces trust must quantify both the saving and the harm and propose mitigation. "It deflects [X]% of contacts" is not an argument; it is a number awaiting an argument.
- Any decision that overrides objective 1 requires **Regional MD + Global Service Head** sign-off and entry in the Exception Register with a review date.
- The Council publishes its decisions. Precedent is how a federated service model stays coherent without a 400-page script library.

---

## §3 The Resolution Rule and the four layers

> **Resolution Rule:** Every customer problem is resolved at the earliest point that can see the whole problem — and no later. Every *policy* about resolution is set at the lowest layer that can see every customer it affects — and no lower.

| Layer | Owner | Scope | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Service Spine** | Global Service Council | 7 promises. Universal, non-waivable. | Annual |
| **Regional Dial** | [Market M] leadership + CX + Legal + Logistics | Channel mix, languages and dialects, hours, remedy menu and values, returns/refund mechanics, payment-failure handling, tone-of-voice guide, escalation ladder, partner SLAs | Quarterly |
| **Journey Charter** | Named cross-functional Journey Owner per contact-intent family (§4) | Root-cause backlog, self-service flow, automation boundary, agent playbook, target metrics, defect SLA on upstream teams | Monthly review, published |
| **Frontline Authority** | Agent, within published guardrails | Resolve, refund, replace, waive, expedite, gift — up to a funded discretion limit, without escalation | Continuous; audited monthly |

### 3.1 The Service Spine (adopt or amend; do not expand)

**P1 — We tell the truth about time.** Every promise we display (delivery, refund, response, repair) is a commitment we measure ourselves against publicly, with an honest confidence range rather than an optimistic point estimate. Under-promise; over-deliver.

**P2 — One contact, one owner.** A customer never re-explains their problem. Ownership transfers with full context; the customer is never the integration layer between our departments.

**P3 — Never a dead end.** Every automated interaction has a visible, one-tap route to a human. Automation may triage, draft, translate and act; it may not trap.

**P4 — The frontline can fix things.** Every agent has published authority to resolve up to a defined value without permission. Escalation is a design failure, tracked as such.

**P5 — Local by default, not translated.** Language, tone, channel, examples, payment methods, address handling and holiday calendars are set locally. Global templates are a starting point, never a requirement.

**P6 — Accessible to everyone who buys from us.** Low-bandwidth paths, voice options where literacy or connectivity demand it, screen-reader compliance, and a channel that works on the devices our customers actually own.

**P7 — Every recurring contact reason has an owner outside the contact centre.** Service reports the defect; the defect's owner is accountable for eliminating it, on a clock.

Seven is the ceiling. Anything added must be simultaneously true, legal, affordable and culturally legible in every market we operate.

---

## §4 The design unit: contact intents, not channels

Organising service by channel (phone team, email team, chat team) guarantees inconsistency, because the *same* problem gets a different answer depending on where the customer knocked. Organise instead by **intent**, and route intent to the treatment it deserves.

| # | Intent | Discriminating test | Correct treatment | Automation suitability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **I1** | **Status anxiety** — "where is my order?" | Customer wants information we already hold | **Eliminate**: proactive push, accurate tracking, live ETA | Full — but the real answer is prevention |
| **I2** | **Transaction change** — reschedule, reroute, cancel, address fix | Customer wants a *state change*, not advice | **Self-serve action**, one tap, instant confirmation | Full, if the flow *acts* rather than explains |
| **I3** | **Something is broken** — wrong, damaged, missing, late, payment failed | A promise was broken | **Human or high-confidence auto-remedy, plus root-cause capture** | Partial; consequence is high |
| **I4** | **Advice and decision help** — sizing, fit, compatibility, comparison | Customer needs judgement to buy | **Assisted commerce** — expert humans, community, rich content | Assist only; converts revenue |
| **I5** | **Trust rupture** — anger, unfairness, repeated failure, public complaint, vulnerability | The relationship is at stake | **Named senior owner, generous fast remedy, follow-up** | **Never automate** |

**The two intents teams confuse:** I1 and I3. "Where is my order" *after* a missed promise is not I1 — it is I3 wearing I1's clothes, and answering it with a tracking link is how a recoverable failure becomes churn. Detection logic for this is a Diagnostic Gate deliverable.

**Design implication:** I1 and I2 are, we believe, the majority of current contact volume in [Market M] — *this is a hypothesis, not a finding*, and it is the Diagnostic Gate's first test. If confirmed, the highest-return investment is not the contact centre at all.

---

## §5 The twelve intervention tracks

Ordered by sequence, not by ambition. Tracks 1–4 pay for the rest.

### Wave 1 — Eliminate failure demand *(weeks 0–12)*

**Track 1 — Contact-reason forensics and defect ownership.**
Re-code the last [12] months of contacts into the I1–I5 taxonomy plus a root-cause layer (carrier, catalogue, payment, policy, UX, our own message). Publish a weekly **Top 20 Contact Reasons** board with a named owner *outside* service for each, a defect SLA *[target: root cause fixed or mitigation shipped within 60 days]*, and a visible cost-of-failure figure per reason. **Innovation is not required here; accountability is.** Expected volume reduction: *[target: 20–30% within two quarters]*.

**Track 2 — Honest promises engine.**
Replace optimistic single-date ETAs with locally calibrated, confidence-ranged promises computed per postcode/partner/product/season. Deliberately pad the customer-facing promise while optimising the internal target; measure **promise-kept rate**, not average delivery time. In markets with volatile last-mile, this single change typically moves satisfaction more than any contact-centre investment.

**Track 3 — Proactive disruption service.**
Detect the failure before the customer does — carrier exception, customs hold, weather event, stock-out, failed payment, address ambiguity — and reach out first with (a) what happened, (b) what we've already done, (c) two choices, (d) a remedy already applied where we were at fault. **The default is not "notify"; it is "notify and resolve in the same message."** Preventing an I1/I3 contact is worth several times containing one.

**Track 4 — Self-service that acts.**
Retire FAQ-as-service. Every I2 intent becomes a one-tap action in-app and in the order confirmation: reschedule, reroute, change address, cancel, return, exchange, split delivery, refund-to-original-method. Embedded contextually at the point of friction, not buried in a help centre. Target: *[80]% of I2 resolved without human contact and without customer effort exceeding [3] taps.*

### Wave 2 — Rebuild assisted service for this market *(weeks 8–24)*

**Track 5 — Channel realism.**

Move the primary assisted channel to **[Market M's dominant messaging platform]** with full commerce and identity integration, asynchronous by design, threaded so history persists and P2 is structurally guaranteed. Hire a small number of **service designers who are from this market**, not global staff on rotation.

**Track 7 — The AI/human boundary, drawn on two axes.**
Automate on **confidence × consequence**, never on cost alone.

- vernacular voice AI / IVR-free voice for low-literacy or low-bandwidth segments;
- **assisted commerce** as revenue service (live video styling/sizing/compatibility consults) — mentioned once in I4 and never developed;

- compensation-by-default ("we broke the promise, the credit is already applied") — hinted in Track 3(d), never given a value framework, funding line or abuse control;
- peer/community answer layers with reputation incentives;
- a published external promise-kept dashboard as a trust instrument, not just an internal metric.

## 4. Substantive analytic problems

**a) Units error in the population table.** A, B and C are defined as shares of *contact volume* and sum to 100%. D ("silent dissatisfied") is then sized at "[2–4]× population C" — but D is a *customer* population, not a contact population, and by definition generates no contacts. The comparison is a category error and will be attacked in the first review. Give D its own denominator (e.g., % of active buyers with a detectable negative signal and no contact).

**b) The Resolution Rule contains two different rules.** "Resolved at the earliest point that can see the whole problem" (an operational routing rule) and "policy set at the lowest layer that can see every customer affected" (a subsidiarity rule) are bolted together and then described as "one constraint." Separate them, or the framework's keystone reads as rhetorical symmetry imported from the source document.

**c) Unreconciled contradiction on escalation.** P4 declares "escalation is a design failure, tracked as such." The request is one regional market with soft feedback. The response erects a four-layer constitution with a non-waivable global Spine, an Exception Register, quarterly Dial reviews, per-intent-family Journey Charters with monthly published reviews, and a Council with published precedent. - **Risk register** — including abuse/fraud exposure created by funded frontline discretion and auto-remedy (mentioned only as "audited monthly"), vendor/BPO contract constraints, and works-council or labour implications of changing frontline authority and channel mix.
- **Vulnerability definition** — invoked in I5 with no definition or regulatory framing, which matters in several jurisdictions.
- **Loyalty measurement** — cohort repeat rate, category expansion, retention curves; CSAT/NPS limitations in low-response or high-courtesy-bias markets are never discussed despite §1's promise to measure "in local terms."

- **Intent taxonomy over channel taxonomy**, and the I1-vs-I3 distinction ("status anxiety after a missed promise is I3 wearing I1's clothes") — a sharp, actionable insight with a clear detection deliverable.

5. Fix the population-D units error; split the Resolution Rule in two; reconcile P4 with I5 on escalation.
6. Downgrade the ETA-padding claim to a bounded, testable hypothesis with a conversion guardrail.
7. Add cost envelope, research design, pilot/control design, and a risk-and-abuse section.
8. Rebalance timeline into 12-week regional quick wins vs platform asks with lead times.
9. Trim inherited rhetoric and reduce governance layers to match a single-market mandate.

Also in scope, and usually omitted: **the frontline agents themselves** (§6). Agent experience is not a welfare topic; it is the single largest controllable input to customer satisfaction, and in this market it is currently a bottleneck.

## §1 Stating the problem correctly

The regional feedback says "support is not meeting expectations." That sentence contains no diagnosis. Reframe it:

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| How do we improve our support channels? | Why are customers contacting us at all, and which contacts are our own defects? |
| How do we reduce response time? | How do we reduce *time to resolution* — and how often do we make the customer come back a second time? |
| Should we add a chatbot? | Which contacts have low consequence and high machine confidence — and which must never touch automation? |
| Are customers satisfied? | Are they *returning*, buying across categories, and telling us the truth — and which segments have gone quiet? |
| What's our CSAT? | What is our CSAT **for the journeys we handle worst**, in the local language, at the local peak? |
| Why is this market underperforming? | Which of our global defaults are simply wrong here — channel, language, payment, returns, tone, hours? |

**Corollary 1 — Contact volume is a defect signal, not a workload forecast.** The default operational reflex is to staff to demand. The correct first reflex is to ask which demand should not exist. Every recurring contact reason is an unpaid invoice from another department.

**Corollary 2 — Most regional dissatisfaction is not a service problem.** It is a **promise problem** (ETAs we cannot keep), a **legibility problem** (policies written for a different market), a **language problem** (translated, not localised), a **channel problem** (we offer email; they live on messaging), or an **authority problem** (agents who must escalate to help). Fixing these is cheaper than expanding the centre, and it compounds. **Sequence them first.**

**Corollary 3 — Satisfaction and loyalty are not the same objective.** Satisfaction is the absence of friction. Loyalty is the presence of reciprocity — a memory of being treated well when it would have been easy to treat us badly. A programme that only removes friction produces indifferent customers who leave for a discount. Tracks 9–12 exist for this reason.

## §2 What we are optimising for

**A gate, not a priority — Regulatory, data and consumer-protection integrity.** No arrangement that breaches [Market M] consumer law (return windows, refund timelines, warranty duties, cooling-off rights), data-residency or privacy rules, marketing-consent rules, accessibility obligations, or any outsourcing/labour agreement covering frontline staff. Applied as pass/fail *before* options are compared. Legal and DPO hold a veto, not an opinion. Automated decisioning that affects a customer's money is in scope of this gate.

**The five ranked objectives**, in priority order when they conflict:

| Rank | Objective | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Trust** | Customers believe our promises (ETA accuracy, refund actually arriving on the day stated) and believe we will make things right |
| **2** | **Effective resolution** | The customer's problem is *gone*, first time, without a second contact |
| **3** | **Effortlessness** | Time and steps the customer spends, measured in *their* terms, not ours |
| **4** | **Relationship depth** | Repeat purchase, category expansion, willingness to be contacted, advocacy |
| **5** | **Cost to serve** | Fully-loaded cost per resolved contact, and per *retained* customer |

Trust outranks resolution because a fast fix inside a system that lies about delivery dates buys nothing. Cost is last because savings taken out of trust are borrowed, not earned — and in this market, evidently, already overdrawn.

### 2.1 Adjudication

- Conflicts are decided by the **Regional Service Council** (§7.1) on a written submission naming the objectives in tension, the evidence, and the customer population affected.
- **Burden of proof sits with the lower-ranked objective.** A containment or automation proposal that reduces trust must quantify both the saving and the harm and propose mitigation. "It deflects [X]% of contacts" is not an argument; it is a number awaiting an argument.
- Any decision that overrides objective 1 requires **Regional MD + Global Service Head** sign-off and entry in the Exception Register with a review date.
- The Council publishes its decisions. Precedent is how a federated service model stays coherent without a 400-page script library.

## §3 The Resolution Rule and the four layers

> **Resolution Rule:** Every customer problem is resolved at the earliest point that can see the whole problem — and no later. Every *policy* about resolution is set at the lowest layer that can see every customer it affects — and no lower.

| Layer | Owner | Scope | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Service Spine** | Global Service Council | 7 promises. Universal, non-waivable. | Annual |
| **Regional Dial** | [Market M] leadership + CX + Legal + Logistics | Channel mix, languages and dialects, hours, remedy menu and values, returns/refund mechanics, payment-failure handling, tone-of-voice guide, escalation ladder, partner SLAs | Quarterly |
| **Journey Charter** | Named cross-functional Journey Owner per contact-intent family (§4) | Root-cause backlog, self-service flow, automation boundary, agent playbook, target metrics, defect SLA on upstream teams | Monthly review, published |
| **Frontline Authority** | Agent, within published guardrails | Resolve, refund, replace, waive, expedite, gift — up to a funded discretion limit, without escalation | Continuous; audited monthly |

### 3.1 The Service Spine (adopt or amend; do not expand)

**P1 — We tell the truth about time.** Every promise we display (delivery, refund, response, repair) is a commitment we measure ourselves against publicly, with an honest confidence range rather than an optimistic point estimate. Under-promise; over-deliver.

**P2 — One contact, one owner.** A customer never re-explains their problem. Ownership transfers with full context; the customer is never the integration layer between our departments.

**P3 — Never a dead end.** Every automated interaction has a visible, one-tap route to a human. Automation may triage, draft, translate and act; it may not trap.

**P4 — The frontline can fix things.** Every agent has published authority to resolve up to a defined value without permission. Escalation is a design failure, tracked as such.

**P5 — Local by default, not translated.** Language, tone, channel, examples, payment methods, address handling and holiday calendars are set locally. Global templates are a starting point, never a requirement.

**P6 — Accessible to everyone who buys from us.** Low-bandwidth paths, voice options where literacy or connectivity demand it, screen-reader compliance, and a channel that works on the devices our customers actually own.

**P7 — Every recurring contact reason has an owner outside the contact centre.** Service reports the defect; the defect's owner is accountable for eliminating it, on a clock.

Seven is the ceiling. Anything added must be simultaneously true, legal, affordable and culturally legible in every market we operate.

## §4 The design unit: contact intents, not channels

Organising service by channel (phone team, email team, chat team) guarantees inconsistency, because the *same* problem gets a different answer depending on where the customer knocked. Organise instead by **intent**, and route intent to the treatment it deserves.

| # | Intent | Discriminating test | Correct treatment | Automation suitability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **I1** | **Status anxiety** — "where is my order?" | Customer wants information we already hold | **Eliminate**: proactive push, accurate tracking, live ETA | Full — but the real answer is prevention |
| **I2** | **Transaction change** — reschedule, reroute, cancel, address fix | Customer wants a *state change*, not advice | **Self-serve action**, one tap, instant confirmation | Full, if the flow *acts* rather than explains |
| **I3** | **Something is broken** — wrong, damaged, missing, late, payment failed | A promise was broken | **Human or high-confidence auto-remedy, plus root-cause capture** | Partial; consequence is high |
| **I4** | **Advice and decision help** — sizing, fit, compatibility, comparison | Customer needs judgement to buy | **Assisted commerce** — expert humans, community, rich content | Assist only; converts revenue |
| **I5** | **Trust rupture** — anger, unfairness, repeated failure, public complaint, vulnerability | The relationship is at stake | **Named senior owner, generous fast remedy, follow-up** | **Never automate** |

**The two intents teams confuse:** I1 and I3. "Where is my order" *after* a missed promise is not I1 — it is I3 wearing I1's clothes, and answering it with a tracking link is how a recoverable failure becomes churn. Detection logic for this is a Diagnostic Gate deliverable.

**Design implication:** I1 and I2 are, we believe, the majority of current contact volume in [Market M] — *this is a hypothesis, not a finding*, and it is the Diagnostic Gate's first test. If confirmed, the highest-return investment is not the contact centre at all.

## §5 The twelve intervention tracks

Ordered by sequence, not by ambition. Tracks 1–4 pay for the rest.

### Wave 1 — Eliminate failure demand *(weeks 0–12)*

**Track 1 — Contact-reason forensics and defect ownership.**
Re-code the last [12] months of contacts into the I1–I5 taxonomy plus a root-cause layer (carrier, catalogue, payment, policy, UX, our own message). Publish a weekly **Top 20 Contact Reasons** board with a named owner *outside* service for each, a defect SLA *[target: root cause fixed or mitigation shipped within 60 days]*, and a visible cost-of-failure figure per reason. **Innovation is not required here; accountability is.** Expected volume reduction: *[target: 20–30% within two quarters]*.

**Track 2 — Honest promises engine.**
Replace optimistic single-date ETAs with locally calibrated, confidence-ranged promises computed per postcode/partner/product/season. Deliberately pad the customer-facing promise while optimising the internal target; measure **promise-kept rate**, not average delivery time. In markets with volatile last-mile, this single change typically moves satisfaction more than any contact-centre investment.

**Track 3 — Proactive disruption service.**
Detect the failure before the customer does — carrier exception, customs hold, weather event, stock-out, failed payment, address ambiguity — and reach out first with (a) what happened, (b) what we've already done, (c) two choices, (d) a remedy already applied where we were at fault. **The default is not "notify"; it is "notify and resolve in the same message."** Preventing an I1/I3 contact is worth several times containing one.

**Track 4 — Self-service that acts.**
Retire FAQ-as-service. Every I2 intent becomes a one-tap action in-app and in the order confirmation: reschedule, reroute, change address, cancel, return, exchange, split delivery, refund-to-original-method. Embedded contextually at the point of friction, not buried in a help centre. Target: *[80]% of I2 resolved without human contact and without customer effort exceeding [3] taps.*

### Wave 2 — Rebuild assisted service for this market *(weeks 8–24)*

**Track 5 — Channel realism.**
Meet customers where they already are. Move the primary assisted channel to **[Market M's dominant messaging platform]** with full commerce and identity integration, asynchronous by design, threaded so history persists and P2 is structurally guaranteed. Retain voice for I3/I5 and for segments that prefer it; retain a low-bandwidth path. **Do not add channels — replace them.** Channel proliferation is how consistency dies.

**Track 6 — Localisation, not translation.**
Native speakers of [Market M languages and principal dialects], locally written tone-of-voice guide (directness, formality, apology conventions, how complaint is culturally expressed), local holiday and peak calendars, local payment-failure playbooks (including cash-on-delivery, instalments, wallet mechanics as applicable), local address-normalisation logic, local returns network (partner stores, lockers, pickup points) instead of an imported courier-only model. | **Low machine confidence** | **Automate triage; human resolves** | **Human only, senior, no bot in the path** (I5) |

## The answer, up front

Regional satisfaction problems are rarely solved by adding agents, extending hours, or adding a chatbot. They are solved by **separating three things that our single queue currently blends together**: contacts caused by our own broken promises; contacts where the customer genuinely needs help or judgement; and contacts where the relationship itself is at stake. Each needs a different design, a different owner, and a different measure of success.

So: (i) **remove the reasons to contact us** — wrong ETAs, opaque returns, silent failures — because that is the cheapest satisfaction we will ever buy; (ii) **rebuild assisted service around how this market actually communicates**, in its language, on its dominant channel, with agents who have the power to fix things without asking permission; then (iii) **convert failures and advice moments into relationship assets** through designed recovery, assisted commerce, local presence and reciprocity — because friction removal alone produces satisfied customers who still leave for a two-percent discount.

Two rules govern the design, and they are deliberately separate:

> **The Resolution Rule (operational).** Every customer problem is resolved at the earliest contact point that can see the whole problem and has authority to act — except where consequence is high, in which case ownership, not speed, governs routing (§3.2).
>
> **The Locality Rule (policy).** Every service policy is set at the lowest layer that can see every customer it affects, and no lower.

*Terminology note: the failure-demand / value-demand distinction used throughout is John Seddon's; we use it as a design lens, not a claim of originality.*

**A gate, not a priority — regulatory, data and consumer-protection integrity.** Nothing that breaches [Market M] consumer law (return windows, refund timelines, warranty duties, cooling-off rights), data-residency or privacy rules, marketing-consent rules, accessibility duties, automated-decisioning rules where a customer's money is affected, or any labour/outsourcing agreement covering frontline staff. Pass/fail, applied before options are compared. Legal and the DPO hold a veto.

**The five ranked objectives**, in priority order when they conflict:

| Rank | Objective | Test |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Trust** | Customers believe our promises (ETA accuracy, refund arriving on the day stated) and believe we will make things right |
| 2 | **Effective resolution** | The problem is gone, first time, without a second contact |
| 3 | **Effortlessness** | Customer time and steps, measured in their terms |
| 4 | **Relationship depth** | Repeat purchase, category expansion, contactability, advocacy |
| 5 | **Cost to serve** | Fully-loaded cost per *resolved* contact, and per *retained* customer |

Trust ranks first because a fast fix inside a system that lies about delivery dates buys nothing durable. Cost ranks last not because it is unimportant but because it is the only objective that improves automatically when the other four are met: eliminating a contact is cheaper than handling it well.

### 2.1 Adjudication

- Conflicts are decided by the **Regional Service Board** (§7.1) on a one-page written submission naming the objectives in tension, the evidence, and the customer population affected.
- **The burden of proof sits with the lower-ranked objective.** A cost or automation proposal that reduces trust must quantify the saving *and* the harm, and propose mitigation. A deflection percentage on its own is a cost claim, not a service case.
- Any decision that overrides Objective 1 requires **Regional MD + Global Service Head** sign-off and an entry in the exception log with a review date.
- The Board publishes its decisions. In a model with this much delegated authority, published precedent is what keeps agents consistent without a script library.

---

## §3 Layers, rules and decision rights

### 3.1 Three layers, not four

We deliberately keep governance thin: this is one market with a soft-feedback problem, not a constitutional crisis. The global-federation apparatus (spine amendment procedures, cross-market exception registers) is deferred to **Appendix C**, to be invoked only if this scales.

| Layer | Owner | Scope | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Service Spine** | Global Service Head | 7 promises. Universal, non-waivable. | Annual |
| **Regional Service Board** (Dial + Council collapsed into one forum) | Regional MD chairs; CX, Ops/Logistics, Product liaison, Legal, Finance, frontline representation | Channel mix, languages, hours, remedy menu and discretion values, returns/refund mechanics, payment-failure handling, tone-of-voice, partner SLAs, priority conflicts, exception decisions | Monthly for 2 quarters, then quarterly |
| **Journey Charter** | A named **Journey Owner** per intent family (§4), cross-functional, with a mandate over the upstream defect and not just the queue | Root-cause backlog, self-service flow, automation boundary, agent playbook, target metrics | Reviewed at the Board monthly; published internally |
| **Frontline Authority** | The agent, within published guardrails | Resolve, refund, replace, waive, expedite, gift — up to a funded limit, without escalation | Decision authority: **continuous**. Audit: **monthly**, by sample (§12.2) |

### 3.2 The two rules, separated

**Resolution Rule (operational routing).** Resolve at the earliest point that can see the whole problem *and* has authority to act. Two named exceptions:
- **Consequence override.** For I5 (trust rupture) and for cases meeting the vulnerability definition (§12.4), *ownership* governs routing, not speed. A named senior owner takes the case immediately; this is a designed assignment, not a failure.
- **Fraud/abuse override.** Cases tripping abuse thresholds (§12.2) route to a specialist path, with the customer told what is happening and by when.

**Locality Rule (policy).** Set policy at the lowest layer that can see every customer it affects. A remedy value affecting only [Market M] belongs to the Board; a promise about how we behave everywhere belongs to the Spine.

### 3.3 The Service Spine — seven promises

**P1 — We tell the truth about time.** Every promise we display (delivery, refund, response, repair) is measured against outcome, with an honest range rather than an optimistic point estimate.

**P2 — One contact, one owner.** A customer never re-explains their problem. Context travels with ownership; the customer is never the integration layer between our departments.

**P3 — Never a dead end.** Every automated interaction has a visible route to a human. Automation may triage, translate, draft and act. It may not trap.

**P4 — The frontline can fix things.** Every agent has published authority to resolve up to a defined value without permission.
*Reconciled with I5:* we distinguish two kinds of handoff. **Transfer-for-authority** — the agent knew the answer but lacked the power — is a design defect and is measured as one. **Assignment-for-ownership** — deliberately moving a high-consequence case to a named senior owner — is the intended pattern and is measured as coverage, not as failure. Only the first counts against the escalation metric.

**P5 — Local by default, not translated.** Language, tone, channel, examples, payment methods, address handling and holiday calendars are set locally. Global templates are a starting point, never a requirement.

**P6 — Reachable by everyone who buys from us.** Low-bandwidth paths, voice options where literacy or connectivity require them, screen-reader compliance, and channels that work on the devices our customers actually own.

**P7 — Every recurring contact reason has a named owner outside the contact centre**, and service has a standing right to place that reason on that owner's backlog (mechanism and escalation path: Appendix B).

Seven is intended as a ceiling: anything added has to hold simultaneously in every market we operate, which very little does.

---

## §4 The design unit: intent, and separately, fault

Organising service by channel (phone team, email team, chat team) produces inconsistency, because the same problem gets a different answer depending on where the customer knocked. Organise by **intent** — what the customer is trying to achieve — and route intent to the treatment it deserves.

### 4.1 Five intents

| # | Intent | Discriminating test | Correct treatment | Automation suitability |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **I1** | **Status anxiety** — "where is my order?" | Customer wants information we already hold | **Eliminate** via proactive push and accurate live ETA | Full — but prevention is the real answer |
| **I2** | **Transaction change** — reschedule, reroute, cancel, address fix, return | Customer wants a *state change*, not advice | **Self-serve action**: one tap, instant confirmation | Full, if the flow *acts* rather than explains |
| **I3** | **Something is wrong** — wrong, damaged, missing, late, payment failed | An expectation was broken (by us, a partner, or the world) | Human or high-confidence auto-remedy, **plus root-cause capture** | Partial; consequence is high |
| **I4** | **Advice and decision help** — sizing, fit, compatibility, comparison | Customer needs judgement in order to buy | **Assisted commerce**: expert humans, community, rich content | Assist only; this is revenue, not cost |
| **I5** | **Trust rupture** — anger, repeated failure, perceived unfairness, public complaint, vulnerability | The relationship is at stake | Named senior owner, fast generous remedy, follow-up | **Never automate the resolution** |

**The confusion that costs us most: I1 vs I3.** "Where is my order?" *after* a missed promise is not status anxiety; it is a broken promise wearing status anxiety's clothes. Answering it with a tracking link is how a recoverable failure becomes churn. Building the detection logic — promise breached, or breach probable, at the moment of contact — is a Gate deliverable and a Wave 1 platform ask.

### 4.2 Fault is a second, independent axis

Intent tells us how to *treat* the contact. Fault tells us who owns *eliminating* it. Conflating the two is how service teams end up demanding that Product fix the weather.

| Fault class | Examples | Counts toward failure-demand reduction target? | Owner of prevention |
|---|---|---|---|
| **F1 Our defect** | Wrong ETA logic, bad catalogue data, broken refund flow, unclear policy copy, our own notification failure | **Yes** | Named upstream owner (P7) |
| **F2 Partner defect under our contract** | Carrier mis-scan, failed delivery attempt, locker outage | **Yes** — we chose the partner | Logistics + Commercial (SLA) |
| **F3 External event** | Customs, weather, strike, bank decline outside our retry logic | **No** — but *communication* about it is F1 if we were silent | Proactive service (Track 3) |
| **F4 Customer-originated** | Mistyped address, wrong size ordered, card expired | **No** — but *design* that makes the error likely is F1 | UX + Journey Owner |
| **F5 Value demand** | Advice, compatibility, gifting help, complex orders | **No** — do not eliminate; monetise (Track 10) | Assisted commerce |

Every re-coded contact carries both an intent code and a fault code. The failure-demand reduction target applies to F1 + F2 only.
